steps.title: Configure Git user and alias
steps.instructions: Set your global Git username and email, verify the settings, and create an alias for git init.

targets.caption: Set your global username, email, and alias in the terminal

explanations.topic: Why git config sets username and email
Creating command aliases with git config

hints: Use git config with the --global flag to set configuration values across repositories.
Set user.name and user.email first, then inspect them with git config --list.
Run git config --global alias.i init to create a shorthand for git init.
common_mistakes: Forgetting --global when intending to configure Git for all repositories on the machine.
Omitting quotes around values that contain spaces.

steps.title: Initialize a new Git repository
steps.instructions: Create a directory named project1, navigate into it, and initialize it as a Git repository.

targets.caption: Run git i (or git init) inside the project1 folder

explanations.topic: What git init does to a regular folder

hints: Create the folder with mkdir and move into it with cd before initializing Git.
You can use the git i alias you just created (or git init) inside project1.
common_mistakes: Running git init in the parent Documents directory instead of inside project1.

steps.title: Create and stage project files
steps.instructions: Create hello.md, learning.py, and waiting.py, then stage hello.md and learning.py while checking status.

targets.caption: Stage a specific file with git add <filename>

explanations.topic: Using git status to inspect tracked and untracked files
Difference between git add . and git add <file name>

hints: Use touch to create empty files in the terminal.
Use git add . to stage all current files, or git add <filename> for a single file.
After creating waiting.py, run git add learning.py and check with git status.
common_mistakes: Running git add . at the end instead of git add learning.py, which stages waiting.py too early.

steps.title: Edit Python file and stage updates
steps.instructions: Open the project in VS Code, add a print statement to learning.py, and stage the updated file.

targets.caption: Add the print statement inside learning.py

explanations.topic: Why modified files must be re-staged with git add

hints: Open VS Code from the terminal using code .
Add print("I am learning git!") to learning.py and save the file.
Run git add learning.py in the terminal to stage the new edit.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to save learning.py in the editor before running git add.
Assuming the earlier git add automatically includes later edits to the file.

steps.title: Commit staged changes to history
steps.instructions: Create an initial commit, add my_function to learning.py, then stage and commit all remaining changes.

targets.caption: Define my_function in learning.py before the second commit
Commit staged files with a descriptive message

explanations.topic: What git commit does and why untracked files stay out

hints: First run git commit -m "initial commit" to store the staged files.
Add def my_function(): with a print statement to learning.py and save it.
Run git add . followed by git commit -m "add waiting file and new function".
common_mistakes: Running git commit without the -m flag and getting stuck in the default text editor.
Forgetting to run git add . before the second commit.

steps.title: Clone a remote GitHub repository
steps.instructions: Clone the GitGoing repository from GitHub to your local machine and change into the gitgoing folder.

targets.caption: Paste the HTTPS URL after git clone

explanations.topic: What cloning a remote repository means

hints: Copy the HTTPS repository URL from the green Code dropdown on GitHub.
Run git clone followed by the URL from your Documents folder, not inside project1.
Use cd gitgoing to move into the newly cloned repository.
common_mistakes: Cloning a repository inside an existing Git repository folder (project1).

steps.title: Create and switch Git branches
steps.instructions: Create and switch to a branch named update-name, list branches, switch to main, then switch back.

targets.caption: Create and check out the update-name branch

explanations.topic: Why teams use branches for new changes

hints: Use git checkout -b <branch-name> to create a branch and switch to it in one command.
Run git branch to see all local branches (press q to exit the pager if needed).
Practice switching with git switch main and then git switch update-name.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the -b flag on git checkout when creating a brand-new branch.
Not pressing q to exit the git branch pager view.

steps.title: Update, commit, and push branch
steps.instructions: Change the heading in index.html to Git Going, commit the edit on update-name, and push to origin.

targets.caption: Update the h1 title inside index.html
Push the local branch commits up to origin

explanations.topic: How git push uploads local commits to a remote repository

hints: Open index.html in VS Code and replace Todo List with Git Going inside the <h1> tag.
Stage and commit the change with git add . and git commit -m "update app name".
Push your branch to GitHub using git push origin update-name.
common_mistakes: Editing index.html while still on the main branch instead of update-name.
Pushing to a repository where you do not have write access instead of your own fork.

steps.title: Pull merged changes and inspect history
steps.instructions: Switch to main, run git pull to fetch the merged PR changes locally, and inspect the latest commit with git show.

targets.caption: Fetch and merge remote updates into local main
Inspect the commit SHA, author, message, and diff

explanations.topic: Why local main stays behind remote until git pull
Reading commit metadata and diffs with git show

hints: First merge the pull request on GitHub, then switch back to main locally with git switch main.
Run git pull to download and merge the remote main updates into your local main.
Run git show to inspect the commit hash, author, date, and message.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to merge the pull request on GitHub before running git pull on main.

steps.title: Delete local and remote branches
steps.instructions: Clean up the merged update-name branch both locally and on the remote origin repository.

targets.caption: Delete the local branch after merging
Delete the branch from the remote repository

hints: Make sure you are on main before deleting update-name.
Use git branch -d update-name to delete the local branch.
Use git push --delete origin update-name to remove the remote branch.
common_mistakes: Trying to delete the update-name branch while it is still the currently checked-out branch.
